title: Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy: Referral Criteria and Pre-Operative Assessment

evidenceAudit.scope: Primary health centre and paediatric doctors in Saudi Arabia deciding when to refer a child for tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy (recurrent tonsillitis, sleep-disordered breathing, peritonsillar abscess), and ear, nose and throat and anaesthetic teams preparing the child before surgery and planning pain control and counselling afterwards. Uses an international consensus on recurrent acute tonsillitis, a Saudi (Taif) review of indications, a guideline-adherence audit and product labels. Not for adult-specific surgery or malignancy.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Health Council tonsillectomy referral guideline was found; the pathway follows an international consensus (2023) and the Saudi Taif study is descriptive.

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery guideline itself could not be opened; its key action statements (counselling, dexamethasone, polysomnography, modifying factors, analgesia) were read only through a 2025 Pakistan audit and the consensus paper, so the exact wording of those statements is not quoted.

The consensus defines the episode-count criteria (7, 5, 3 episodes) mainly for recurrent acute tonsillitis; criteria for sleep-disordered breathing (polysomnography thresholds, tonsil size grading) were not found in a fetched source and are not written as numbers.

Polysomnography is recommended by the American guideline for some children with sleep-disordered breathing, but access is limited in resource-limited settings (as in the Pakistan audit); no Saudi access data were found, and a validated screening scale (STBUR) is mentioned as an alternative without its scoring.
Intraoperative intravenous dexamethasone is rated grade A in the consensus table, but no dexamethasone label or paediatric dose was read, so no regimen is written; it is for the anaesthetic team.
Peri-operative antibiotics: the audit notes entrenched practice and cites a study finding no benefit of postoperative amoxicillin; no Saudi protocol was found, so no antibiotic regimen is written.

Paracetamol (acetaminophen) and ibuprofen doses are from United States over-the-counter children's labels that give weight and age bands for 2 to 11 years and say to ask a doctor for children under 2 years or under 24 pounds; a per-kilogram dose was not found.
Figures were read by automated extraction of article and label text; spot-check each figure and dose against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Recurrent acute tonsillitis means repeated distinct episodes of bacterial infection of the palatine tonsils with symptom-free intervals; the old term chronic tonsillitis is obsolete (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Definition of recurrent acute tonsillitis and tonsil surgery). Group A Streptococcus is the main bacterial cause and sore throat scores (Centor, McIsaac, FeverPAIN) only estimate its probability (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Clinical assessment of recurrent acute tonsillitis). In children, tonsillectomy gives a small benefit: about 0.6 fewer sore throat episodes in the first year in the Cochrane review (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis). Common indications in children are recurrent tonsillitis and sleep-disordered breathing (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract). Tonsillectomy is among the most painful common procedures, with typical pain scores of 5 to 6 on a 0 to 10 scale for 3 to 5 days (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management).

symptoms: Repeated sore throat with fever, tender neck glands and tonsil pus (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract).
Snoring, pauses in breathing and disturbed sleep in sleep-disordered breathing (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract).

Impact on school attendance and quality of life, which should be counted for each episode (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
physicalSigns: Tonsillar swelling and exudate, cervical lymphadenopathy and fever (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 1).
Large obstructing tonsils graded by the Brodsky scale (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Surgical treatment).
Peritonsillar abscess in the history (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
redFlags: Suspected obstructive sleep apnoea: assess with polysomnography where available before surgery because it affects anaesthetic risk (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Discussion).
More than one peritonsillar abscess is a modifying factor favouring tonsillectomy (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis (PFAPA) is a modifying factor favouring tonsillectomy (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
After surgery: primary and secondary bleeding are the main risk and need urgent review (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Surgical techniques).
Never give codeine to children; opioids only as rescue (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management).
precipitants: Passive smoking, air pollution and infectious exposures (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Introduction).
Age: most surgery is combined adenotonsillectomy in young children (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract).
Previous peritonsillar abscess (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
Recurrent infection in school-age children with frequent school absence (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Low Centor, McIsaac or FeverPAIN score; cough and runny nose; no need for antibiotics (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 1).
Fever, no cough, tonsillar exudate and neck glands; confirmed by a rapid swab (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Clinical assessment of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
Severe unilateral pain and a swollen tonsil; a surgical indication when recurrent (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
Snoring and apnoeas with large tonsils or adenoids; polysomnography confirms obstructive sleep apnoea (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract).
Periodic fevers with aphthous ulcers and pharyngitis; tonsillectomy is a modifying factor (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess each sore throat episode
actions: Take a history, examine the throat and score with Centor, McIsaac or FeverPAIN (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Clinical assessment of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
Do a point-of-care swab test if the score is high (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Clinical assessment of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
Record each episode, whether it was disabling and whether antibiotics were given (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat conservatively
actions: Give paracetamol with or without a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for pain (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Conservative treatment).
Use antibiotics only when bacterial infection is probable (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Results).

clinicalManagement.title: Count episodes and decide on referral
actions: Refer to ear, nose and throat if there have been 7 or more treated episodes in a year, 5 or more per year for 2 years, or 3 or more per year for 3 years (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
Refer a child with suspected sleep-disordered breathing or with a peritonsillar abscess history for specialist assessment (Taif tonsillectomy indications study, Section Abstract).
Record a quality-of-life score (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

clinicalManagement.title: Pre-operative assessment
actions: Check modifying factors: PFAPA, more than one peritonsillar abscess, multiple antibiotic allergy or intolerance (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
Assess for obstructive sleep apnoea and arrange polysomnography where indicated and available (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Discussion).

Counsel the family about the operation, pain for 3 to 5 days and the bleeding risk (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management; AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Results).
Refer to the anaesthetic team for the child's perioperative plan, including intraoperative dexamethasone (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Operate and manage pain
actions: Perform bilateral tonsillectomy by the technique the surgeon is trained in; no technique is clearly better (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Surgical techniques).

Give non-opioid analgesics during surgery and continue afterwards; use opioids only as rescue and never codeine in children (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management).
Use paracetamol plus ibuprofen after surgery unless contraindicated (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow up
actions: Check for primary and secondary bleeding during the first two weeks (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Materials and methods).
Reassess residual sleep-disordered breathing symptoms, as 18% of patients had residual sleep apnoea symptoms after surgery in one study (AAO-HNS adherence audit, Section Discussion).

regimens.patientGroup: Children aged 2 to 11 years (use weight where known)
regimens.genericName: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) oral suspension 160 mg per 5 mL
regimens.dose: By weight band, or age if weight is unknown: 24 to 35 lb (2 to 3 years) 5 mL; 36 to 47 lb (4 to 5 years) 7.5 mL; 48 to 59 lb (6 to 8 years) 10 mL; 60 to 71 lb (9 to 10 years) 12.5 mL; 72 to 95 lb (11 years) 15 mL (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions). Under 24 lb or under 2 years: ask a doctor. Dilution and preparation: none; shake well and measure with the dosing cup (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions).
regimens.frequency: Every 4 hours while symptoms last; no more than 5 doses in 24 hours (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions)
regimens.duration: Typically 3 to 5 days when pain is highest; stop and ask a doctor if pain gets worse or lasts more than 5 days (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management; Children's acetaminophen label, Stop use and ask a doctor)
adjustments: Liver disease: ask a doctor before use (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
Do not combine with another acetaminophen-containing product (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Total acetaminophen in 24 hours (Children's acetaminophen label, Directions).
Pain scores and ability to drink (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management).
Skin reaction: stop and seek help (Children's acetaminophen label, Warnings).
contraindications: Allergy to acetaminophen or an inactive ingredient (Children's acetaminophen label, Do not use).

regimens.patientGroup: Children aged 2 to 11 years (use weight where known)
regimens.genericName: Ibuprofen oral suspension 100 mg per 5 mL
regimens.dose: By weight band, or age if weight is unknown: 24 to 35 lb (2 to 3 years) 5 mL; 36 to 47 lb (4 to 5 years) 7.5 mL; 48 to 59 lb (6 to 8 years) 10 mL; 60 to 71 lb (9 to 10 years) 12.5 mL; 72 to 95 lb (11 years) 15 mL (Children's ibuprofen label, Directions). Under 24 lb or under 2 years: ask a doctor. Dilution and preparation: none; shake well and use only the enclosed dosing cup (Children's ibuprofen label, Directions).
regimens.route: Oral; take with food or milk if the stomach is upset (Children's ibuprofen label, Directions)
regimens.frequency: If needed, repeat every 6 to 8 hours; no more than 4 times a day (Children's ibuprofen label, Directions)
regimens.duration: Short course while pain lasts, guided by the surgeon; the consensus found no evidence that nonsteroidal drugs raise postoperative bleeding risk (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Postoperative pain management)
adjustments: Ask a doctor before use if the child has not been drinking, has lost fluid by vomiting or diarrhoea, has asthma, high blood pressure, heart, liver or kidney disease, or takes a diuretic (Children's ibuprofen label, Warnings).
Stomach bleeding risk is higher with previous ulcers or bleeding problems, anticoagulants, steroids or other anti-inflammatory drugs (Children's ibuprofen label, Warnings).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of stomach bleeding: faintness, vomiting blood, black stools, persistent stomach pain (Children's ibuprofen label, Stop use and ask a doctor).
Oral intake and hydration after surgery (Children's ibuprofen label, Warnings).
Any bleeding from the throat: urgent surgical review (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Surgical techniques).
contraindications: Previous allergic reaction to ibuprofen or another pain reliever or fever reducer (Children's ibuprofen label, Do not use).
Right before or after heart surgery (Children's ibuprofen label, Do not use).

branches.label: Pain after tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy in a child
branches.entryCriteria: Child aged 2 years or older after tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy, able to swallow liquids, with no allergy to either medicine; under 2 years only on a doctor's instruction.

medicationPlan.note: Two over-the-counter analgesics are written for pain after tonsillectomy, used together as the first choice in the consensus (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 4). Doses are taken from United States children's labels. Intraoperative dexamethasone and opioid rescue are for the anaesthetic and surgical team and are not written (see unverified). SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 7 or more adequately treated episodes in the preceding year, 5 or more in each of the preceding 2 years, or 3 or more in each of the preceding 3 years (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

Disabling sore throat that prevented normal functioning (school) and was treated with antibiotics (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Sore throat scores that justify a swab
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Centor 3 to 4, McIsaac 3 to 4 or FeverPAIN 3 to 5 (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Clinical assessment of recurrent acute tonsillitis).

Bilateral tonsillectomy; tonsillotomy for recurrent tonsillitis only in trials, but partial removal is an accepted alternative for sleep-related disorders in children (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Surgical treatment).

Tonsillectomy Outcome Inventory 14 or Tonsil and Adenoid Health Status Instrument, partly validated in Arabic (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Section Classification of the severity of recurrent acute tonsillitis).
Paracetamol plus a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug as first choice; opioid only as rescue (Recurrent acute tonsillitis consensus, Table 4).

teaching.scope: Primary health centre and paediatric doctors in Saudi Arabia deciding when to refer a child for tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy (recurrent tonsillitis, sleep-disordered breathing, peritonsillar abscess), and ear, nose and throat and anaesthetic teams preparing the child before surgery and planning pain control and counselling afterwards. learningObjectives: Count and document treated episodes before referral.
Use sore throat scores and swabs to confirm bacterial episodes.
Assess sleep-disordered breathing and quality of life.
Plan paracetamol plus ibuprofen for pain; no codeine.
pitfalls: Not counselling about 3 to 5 days of pain and bleeding.
keyPoints: Watchful waiting is the default below the episode thresholds.
Do not give codeine to children.
Tonsillotomy for recurrent tonsillitis only in trials.

patientEducation: Most sore throats get better by themselves. We count how many infections your child has to decide whether surgery will help.
Keep a diary of each sore throat with the date, fever, missed school and whether antibiotics were given.
After surgery the throat will be painful for 3 to 5 days; give pain medicine regularly as advised.
Go to the hospital at once if there is bleeding from the mouth.
Some children continue to snore after surgery, so tell us if breathing problems remain.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep your child away from tobacco smoke.
Encourage drinking and soft foods after surgery.
Follow the plan for return to school given by the surgical team.
mdtReferrals: Primary care doctor; paediatrician; ear, nose and throat surgeon; anaesthetist; sleep medicine physician; nurse; pharmacist.
dischargeCriteria: Child drinking and passing urine; pain controlled with the regular analgesic plan; no bleeding; family counselled on bleeding signs, diet and school return; contact number and follow-up arranged.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review in the first two weeks for bleeding and pain, then reassess residual sleep-disordered breathing and sore throat frequency at the surgical follow-up.
